chapterNote: The book turns from diagnosis to charge. Since you cannot know which venture will prosper, which cloud will burst, or what evil is coming on the earth, the Preacher's counsel is not caution but boldness with open hands: send your bread out over the waters, divide your portion seven and eight ways, sow morning and evening both. The farmer who waits on perfect wind never sows, and the one who studies clouds never reaps — ignorance of God's work, as hidden as breath entering the bones of an unborn child, is a reason to act widely, not to freeze. Then the counsel warms into sunlight: light is sweet, rejoice through many years, and remember the dark days are coming so that the bright ones are actually tasted. The closing charge to the young man is the boldest sentence in the book: rejoice in your youth, walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes — and know that for all of it God will bring you into judgment. Joy and judgment are not rivals; the second is what makes the first serious.

1.text: Send your bread out across the face of the waters, for after many days you will find it again.
1.amp: Cast [shalach — send out, release] your bread [lechem] upon the face of ['upon the face of the waters', panim, the KJV margin] the waters [mayim]: for you shall find [matsa] it after many [rob] days [yom].
1.notes: shalach (H7971) is to send out and release, not to discard: grain shipped over seas in trade, or generosity released without a receivable. Either way the counsel is the same venture of faith — let it go beyond your control, and matsa (H4672), the finding, comes back on God's calendar (cf. v. 2; Proverbs 19:17).

2.text: Divide your portion among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what evil may yet come on the earth.
2.amp: Give [natan] a portion [cheleq] to seven [sheba], and also to eight [shemoneh]; for you know [yada] not what evil [ra] shall be upon the earth [eretz].
2.notes: The seven-and-eight formula means 'amply, and then one more': diversify the cheleq (H2506), whether as generosity to many or ventures spread wide. Ignorance of coming ra (H7451) argues for open hands, not clenched ones — you cannot hedge what you cannot foresee, but you can scatter.

3.text: If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves out on the earth; and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it lies.
3.amp: If the clouds [av] be full [male] of rain [geshem], they empty [ruq] themselves upon the earth [eretz]: and if the tree [ets] fall [naphal] toward the south [darom], or toward the north [tsaphon], in the place [maqom] where the tree falls, there it shall be [havah].
3.notes: Two pictures of what is out of your hands: full clouds will burst when they burst, and the fallen ets (H6086) lies where naphal (H5307) left it. Nature runs on fixed appointments man neither schedules nor reverses — the premise for verse 4's rebuke of the weather-watcher.

4.text: The one who keeps watching the wind will never sow, and the one who keeps studying the clouds will never reap.
4.amp: He that observes [shamar — watches, keeps his eye on] the wind [ruach] shall not sow [zara]; and he that regards [raah] the clouds [av] shall not reap [qatsar].
4.notes: shamar (H8104), the guarding-word, misapplied to the sky: perpetual condition-checking as a way of never committing. zara (H2232) and qatsar (H7114), sowing and reaping, both die on the same waiting — perfect weather is the excuse indecision gives itself.

5.text: Just as you do not know the way of the wind, or how the bones take form in the womb of a mother with child, so you do not know the work of God, who makes everything.
5.amp: As you know [yada] not what is the way [derek] of the spirit [ruach — the wind, the breath], nor how the bones [etsem] do grow in the womb [beten] of her that is with child: even so you know not the works [maaseh] of God [Elohim] who makes [asah] all.
5.notes: ruach (H7307) is deliberately double here, wind and breath-of-life both, and the etsem (H6106) forming unseen in the beten (H990) is its quietest miracle (cf. Psalm 139:13-15; John 3:8). The argument runs forward: mystery is not a reason to stall but the very condition under which all sowing is done.

6.text: In the morning sow your seed, and at evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will turn out good.
6.amp: In the morning [boqer] sow [zara] your seed [zera], and in the evening [erev] withhold [yanach] not your hand [yad]: for you know [yada] not whether shall prosper ['shall be right', kasher, the KJV margin], either this or that, or whether they both [shenayim] shall be alike [echad] good [tov].
6.notes: boqer to erev (H1242, H6153): the whole working day, both ends sown. kasher (H3787), to succeed or be right, is the same rare verb as the axe-proverb of 10:10 — and since no one knows which sowing carries it, breadth of effort is wisdom's answer to ignorance. Note the door left open: both may prosper.

7.text: Truly the light is sweet, and it is a pleasant thing for the eyes to see the sun.
7.amp: Truly the light [or] is sweet [mathoq], and a pleasant [tov] thing it is for the eyes [ayin] to behold [raah] the sun [shemesh].
7.notes: mathoq (H4966), sweet to the taste: light enjoyed the way honey is. After ten chapters of 'under the sun' as a limit, the shemesh itself is suddenly a gift — plain daylight, plainly delighted in, is the book's own proof that vapor and sweetness coexist.

8.text: So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in every one of them — and let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. All that is coming is vapor.
8.amp: But if a man [adam] live [chayah] many [rabah] years [shanah], and rejoice [samach] in them all; yet let him remember [zakar] the days [yom] of darkness [choshek]; for they shall be many [rabah]. All that comes [bo] is vapor [hebel].
8.notes: Both imperatives at full strength: samach (H8055) in all the years, and zakar (H2142) the choshek (H2822) ahead — old age and the grave. Remembering the dark is not morbidity; it is what makes the present light taste like verse 7. The hebel-refrain tolls once more over everything still to come.

9.text: Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart do you good in the days of your prime. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes — and know this, that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
9.amp: Rejoice [samach], O young man [bachur — a man in his prime vigor], in your youth [yalduth]; and let your heart [leb] cheer [tob] you in the days [yom] of your youth, and walk [halak] in the ways [derek] of your heart, and in the sight [mareh] of your eyes [ayin]: but know [yada] you, that for all these things God [Elohim] will bring [bo] you into judgment [mishpat].
9.notes: The bachur (H970) is the young man at full strength, and the charge is real, not ironic: samach, walk, see, taste. The hinge is yada (H3045) — joy lived in the knowledge of mishpat (H4941) is freedom with a keel; the judgment-clause does not cancel the rejoicing, it consecrates it (cf. 12:14).

10.text: So put vexation out of your heart and put away evil from your flesh, for childhood and the dawn of life are vapor.
10.amp: Therefore remove [sur — turn aside] sorrow [kaas — vexation, 'anger', the KJV margin] from your heart [leb], and put away [abar — make pass over] evil [ra] from your flesh [basar]: for childhood [yalduth] and youth [shacharuth — the dawn of life, the black-haired years] are vapor [hebel].
10.notes: Two removals, inward and outward: sur (H5493) the kaas (H3708) from the leb, abar (H5674) the ra from the basar. shacharuth (H7839) is the dawn-word, youth as the morning-dark hours before the day — gone as fast as any hebel, which is exactly why it must not be spent brooding or sinning.
